core: The Nutrition Facts label is the standardized panel on packaged foods and drinks that lists serving size, calories, and nutrient amounts per serving, with a footnote explaining the %DV and the calories used for general nutrition advice
Parts named and how to read each: serving size (typical amount, not a recommendation), servings per container, calories (energy in one serving), nutrients (grams/mg/mcg per serving), %DV, footnote
% Daily Value: the percentage of a daily reference amount (Daily Value) that one serving contributes; 5% DV or less is low, 20% DV or more is high (FDA general guide)
Serving size vs. what you actually eat: every label number is per serving, so multiply by the servings eaten (original worked example, arithmetic verified)
The footnote: explains the %DV and states that 2,000 calories a day is used for general nutrition advice - a general reference, not a personal target
Limits of the label: it appears on packaged foods and drinks; loose fresh foods generally carry no panel
Honest framing: the label is a map of the food, not a judge of the eater; it reports, it does not rank
supporting: History: the Nutrition Labeling and Education Act of 1990 prompted packaged-food labeling with nutrition information and serving sizes (OpenStax)
2016 FDA update: added sugars, vitamin D, and potassium added; serving sizes updated to reflect typical consumption; first major label update in over 20 years
Format variations: dual-column labels on larger packages; trans fat, total sugars, and usually protein carry no %DV
outOfScope: Portion-size guidance and how to measure portions -> nutrition:foundations:portion-sizes (own topic)
What calories are and per-gram energy values -> nutrition:foundations:energy-and-calories (own topic)
Evaluating 'healthy' claims and marketing language -> nutrition:foundations:evaluating-nutrition-claims (own topic)

claims.claim: The Nutrition Facts label is the standardized panel on packaged foods and drinks; its top section lists product-specific information (serving size, calories, and nutrient amounts) and its bottom section is a footnote explaining the %DV and the calories used for general nutrition advice.
Every nutrient amount on the label, including calories, refers to one serving of the food; eating two servings means two times the calories, nutrients, and %DVs shown.

Serving sizes on the label are based on the amount people typically eat and drink, shown in a familiar household measure (cups, pieces, tablespoons) with the metric amount, and are not a recommendation of how much to eat or drink.

The %DV shows how much a nutrient in a serving of food contributes to a total daily diet; Daily Values are reference amounts (in grams, milligrams, or micrograms) of nutrients to consume or not to exceed each day.

As a general guide, 5% DV or less of a nutrient per serving is considered low and 20% DV or more per serving is considered high; the guide supports choosing foods higher in fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, and potassium and lower in saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars.

The label footnote explains how much a nutrient in a serving of food contributes to a daily diet and that 2,000 calories a day is used for general nutrition advice; calorie needs vary by age, sex, height, weight, and physical activity level.

In 2016 the FDA updated the Nutrition Facts label for packaged foods and drinks - the first major update in over 20 years - adding added sugars, vitamin D, and potassium, updating serving sizes to reflect typical consumption, and updating the footnote.
The Nutrition Labeling and Education Act of 1990 prompted all food packaging entities to label foods with nutritional information and serving sizes.
Some label entries carry no %DV: trans fat and total sugars have no %DV, and protein generally has no %DV, so those nutrients are read by their gram amounts.

Worked example (author-constructed, arithmetic verified): an oatmeal-cookie label shows serving size 2 cookies (32 g), 10 servings per container, 160 calories, 7 g total fat (9% DV), 115 mg sodium (5% DV), and 9 g added sugars (18% DV) per serving; eating 6 cookies is 3 servings: 480 calories, 21 g fat (27% DV), 345 mg sodium (15% DV), and 27 g added sugars (54% DV).

conflictingEvidence.issue: No substantive conflict found among FDA, MedlinePlus, and OpenStax on the label's parts, the %DV definition, the 5%/20% guideposts, or the 2,000-calorie footnote.
positions: FDA pages (content current as of 03/05/2024) describe the current standardized label format, including added sugars and the updated footnote.
Labels produced before the 2016 update lack some current features (e.g., added sugars) and used older Daily Values.
MedlinePlus and FDA agree on the packaged-food scope and the 5%/20% guideposts.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the current standardized FDA format and notes that label formats vary (dual-column labels, single-ingredient sugar labels), without claiming all packages look identical.
